articles.title: Center on Budget and Policy spokesperson explains potential harm of proposed SNAP cuts
articles.text:
Center on Budget and Policy spokesperson explains potential harm of proposed SNAP cuts  – WABE
Center on Budget and Policy spokesperson explains potential harm of proposed SNAP cuts
Closer Look
Community
Food
SNAP
Center on Budget and Policy spokesperson explains potential harm of proposed SNAP cuts
Food
LaShawn Hudson
| WABE
November 20th, 2026
It's estimated that 6.3 million people could lose Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits if two newly proposed rules from the U.S. Department of Agriculture are implemented.(Brookings)
Data shows that one of the biggest drivers of turnout in this election cycle was affordability—including everyday costs such as gas, food, and housing.
Since July of last year, when President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill became law, more than five million people have lost their benefits for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, also known as SNAP.
Fast-forward to now, it’s estimated that 6.3 million people could lose their benefits if two newly proposed rules from the U.S. Department of Agriculture are implemented. One rule would change eligibility, and the other would restrict state work-requirement waivers for SNAP.
It’s something that Ty Jones Cox, the vice president for food assistance at the Center on Budget and Policy, says doesn’t make sense.
“The public really indicated they wanted their elected officials to focus on making life more affordable,” Jones Cox said. “And what we’re seeing is that instead of taking actions that can make it more affordable where families can purchase groceries, this administration has chosen, on top of making the biggest cut to SNAP from, following up on the big beautiful bill, is to also propose two rules that’ll further make it harder for families to purchase food.”
As a guest on Friday’s edition of “ Closer Look,” Jones Cox talked candidly with show host Rose Scott about the struggles everyday people, including veterans, are currently navigating and how those struggles could be exacerbated if the new rules are implemented.
“ Maybe have the family of four with $45-46,000 of annual income, but they’re paying for childcare, and they are living somewhere where right now we know rent and mortgage is so high — so that could easily eat into their income, and then they would have to make difficult choices between feeding their families or paying for their shelter costs,” she explained.
Supporters of the proposed USDA rules say the SNAP cuts will save the U.S. more than $50 billion over the next few years and put measures in place to stop and prevent fraud.
“ We are really willing to make 30 million people have to potentially be cut off or have to go through additional barriers?” said Jones Cox. “I think that’s really what it’s about, is that remembering that SNAP covers millions of people, and we’re not making huge changes to a program to stop potential a few bad actors.”
As for what’s next, the proposed rules have to go through a comment period.
“Both of these rules have very short 30-day comment periods, which is not typical,” Jones Cox explained. “Usually, they get a 60-day comment period. So, one big thing is giving people more time to make comments. At the end of the day, though, I hope that these rules are rescinded because on top of the changes that states have to make based on the big beautiful bill, where there’s a cost shift, where states are gonna now have to face potentially millions of dollars by covering benefits, these work requirements that are placed on households, at the end of the day, I am hoping that they are rescinded because this is not the time when families are asking about making life more affordable to have two rules that do the exact opposite.”
During the conversation, Jones Cox doubled down on why she believes the proposed rules aren’t good for all parties involved.
”It’s bad for state agencies; it’s bad for participants,” she said.

articles.title: Food Well Alliance helps metro Atlanta cities grow stronger local food systems
articles.text:
Food Well Alliance helps metro Atlanta cities grow stronger local food systems – WABE
Food Well Alliance helps metro Atlanta cities grow stronger local food systems
Closer Look
Community
Food
Food Aid
Food Insecurity
Metro Atlanta
The State of Our Table
Food Well Alliance helps metro Atlanta cities grow stronger local food systems
Food Aid
Rose Scott
| WABE
November 20th, 2026
On Friday's "Closer Look with Rose Scott," Kate Conner, Executive Director of Food Well Alliance, discussed regional efforts to build equitable and thriving community gardens, urban farms, and orchards across metro Atlanta. (LaShawn Hudson/WABE)
The United States is several generations removed from a time when households primarily relied on growing their own food. Decades ago, families produced much of what they needed for their tables on their own property.
“Two generations ago, a lot more people were growing food. According to the USDA, about 100 years ago, 40% of Americans lived on farms. Today, it’s less than 1%. And not just farming, but gardening as well. We were doing a lot more of that,” said Kate Connor.
As food systems in the United States have evolved, Connor says public policy and urban development have also played a role.
“I think policy and city planning have certainly impacted that, but I also think it reflects a broader change in lifestyle,” she said.
Connor is the executive director of Food Well Alliance, an Atlanta-based nonprofit dedicated to strengthening communities through local food systems. The organization’s mission is to provide resources and support to local growers while helping connect communities through healthy food access.
During an interview with “ Closer Look” host Rose Scott, Connor explained that the organization focuses on three primary areas. The first is supporting growers by providing resources such as compost, grants, seedlings, and equipment. The second is local food system planning.
“We work with cities to support the development of local food systems,” Connor said.
The third is connecting people to food through public events and educational programs. These initiatives introduce community members to topics such as gardening, beekeeping, and other aspects of local food production.
The local food system planning initiative involves residents partnering with their city governments to propose food-related projects. Participating cities must agree to match the funding provided by Food Well Alliance. There are 52 eligible cities in the Atlanta area.
“We work with cities to develop comprehensive plans that support local food systems,” Connor said.
Typically, a city representative and a community member collaborate to identify local needs and develop projects that address them. Once approved, the projects receive implementation funding through a substantial grant.
This year marks the eighth year of the Local Food System Planning initiative. According to Connor, the organization and its partner cities have worked together to implement food-related projects.
“Across the eight cities we’ve worked with, we’ve completed more than 180 projects to support these communities,” she said.
Past projects have included urban gardens, mini farmers markets, and community composting programs. Every year, the organization presents Soil Festival, an annual urban agriculture event celebrating healthy soil, local food leaders, and community gardening.
“So, you name it, we’re doing it,” Connor said. “It’s really driven by what the community wants to see.”
This conversation was part of “Closer Look’s” new series, “ The State of Our Table: Atlanta’s Food Reality.” It’s a deeper dive into how food is connected to economic development, public health, equity, culture, entrepreneurship, environmental sustainability, and the overall health of a community.

articles.title: Why the U.S. air traffic control system relies on an 'antique' network
articles.text:
Why the U.S. air traffic control system relies on an 'antique' network
Why the U.S. air traffic control system still relies on an ‘antique’ network
Transportation
Why the U.S. air traffic control system still relies on an 'antique' network
Transportation
Joel Rose
Joe Hernandez
NPR
November 20th, 2026
CEO Ed Bastian told CNN he will encourage current employees to get vaccinated but won’t require it “if there is some philosophical issue they have” against getting the shots.
Wilfredo Lee / Associated Press file
Rossana D’Antonio was at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York, just about to board a plane back to Los Angeles, when the Federal Aviation Administration declared a nationwide ground stop.
D’Antonio’s flight was canceled last Friday, along with thousands of others. She was lucky, and got a seat on a flight Saturday morning.
“By then, of course, the hotels were all booked. And so I spent the night at JFK,” she said with a rueful laugh.
D’Antonio is not just a frequent flier. She also is the president-elect of the American Society of Civil Engineers. So her mind went right to infrastructure.
“The very first thing I thought of was, ‘We told you so,'” D’Antonio told NPR. “We are reliant on a system that was considered to be state of the art back in the 1980s. This is common knowledge. We’ve known about it, and we simply haven’t acted swiftly enough.”
Last week’s nationwide ground stop was an unwelcome reminder that the U.S.’ air traffic control system runs on antiquated technology.
“We have a patchwork, archaic federal telephone network,” the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, Bryan Bedford, said Thursday at Honeywell Aerospace’s American Aviation Leadership Summit in Washington. “Which is why we gotta get off [of] it as fast as humanly possible, while maintaining safety.”
The FAA is still unsure exactly what caused the telecommunications meltdown that led to the nationwide ground stop, just the second since 9/11. But the agency says it started with work to install a router at a remote facility in Arkansas — part of an ongoing effort to replace outdated copper wiring with modern fiber-optic cables.
No one disputes that the old equipment is a problem, or that updates now underway should have happened a long time ago. So why is the world’s busiest and most complex airspace still running on network technology from the 1980s?
Former FAA and DOT officials say the answer starts with decades of underfunding.
“At its core, it’s a money problem,” Michael Huerta, a former FAA administrator during the Obama administration, said in an interview last year. “The FAA has been asked to do more with less.”
The agency has tried to invest in new technology. But at the same time, Huerta said, the older systems must stay running to keep planes in the air 365 days a year, 24 hours a day.
The older networks are fragile, and expensive to maintain because they’re obsolete, former FAA officials say. And it’s challenging to connect them with modern equipment designed to run on fiber-optic networks.
“This should have been taken on earlier,” said William Voss, a former FAA executive involved in previous modernization efforts back in the 1990s. “It’s effectively been eating all the money up trying to run this antique store in the biggest air traffic system in the world.”
The FAA got an influx of money last year when Congress allocated $12.5 billion to upgrade the air traffic control system. But Voss warned the task is complicated and daunting.
“There’s not a lot of people that have done that in one big leap,” he said.
Voss worries the Trump administration is moving too quickly, without allowing enough time for planning and coordination. And he wonders why the failed network upgrade that crippled the nation’s airspace was scheduled during a busy Friday afternoon.
“I can’t imagine why you do that unless you are just under tremendous schedule pressure,” Voss said.
The timing also seems questionable to Dave Spero. He’s the national president of Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, the union that represents technicians at the FAA.
“No, I wouldn’t do that on a Friday afternoon,” he said. “To be safe, I would probably want to schedule it on a midnight shift.”
The Government Accountability Office also raised concerns about the speed of modernization work. In a report published in September, the GAO said the administration has been accelerating the timeline of modernization work already underway — including the telecommunications network that failed on Friday.
“They are basically buying speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and the potential for disruptions in the national airspace,” said Kevin Walsh, the director of the GAO’s Information Technology and Cybersecurity team, who was the lead on the report.
The GAO report also noted the first phase of the FAA’s modernization effort includes more than 11,000 distinct projects with no integrated master plan.
“While that may work, it increases the risk of outages, especially when dealing with these older systems, which are prone to failure,” Walsh said.
But the Trump administration defends its approach.
“Some of you will say I’m moving too fast. Some of you say, I’m moving too slow. Um, maybe I’m Goldilocks and I’m going just right here,” said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy after meeting Republican Senators at the Capitol on Tuesday. “But I’ll just tell you, the longer we stay on an old rickety network, the less safe it becomes.”
There’s another reason, experts say, the Trump administration might want to move quickly.
After decades of air traffic control modernization attempts that took longer and delivered less than promised, the FAA wants to show Congress that it’s serious this time, said Eric Soskin, a former inspector general at the Department of Transportation.
“That’s a powerful signal to say, hey, we’re going to get it done. We are going to carry out this important effort,” Soskin said.
The FAA still has a lot of modernization work left to do

articles.title: Two reasons people think recent tech failures must be connected
articles.text:
Two reasons people think recent tech failures must be connected
Two reasons people think recent tech failures must be connected: Our brains and online platforms
Biology
National News
Technology
Two reasons people think recent tech failures must be connected: Our brains and online platforms
Biology
Madison Czopek
PolitiFact
November 20th, 2026
An ATM machine displays a "not working" screen at a Chase bank in Irving, Texas, Monday, Nov. 16, 2026. (AP Photo/LM Otero)
It’s been one thing after another.
Companies including Microsoft, United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase and U.S. Bank experienced technical issues and outages that caused widespread banking issues, delayed plane departures and interrupted workdays across the world. Soon after, Marriott and Apple customers also experienced digital problems, and 178 companies reported being affected by a Nov. 16 cyberattack.
At the same time, various U.S. government systems — the Federal Aviation Administration, National Security Agency and National Weather Service — fell into disarray, including a rare nationwide ground stop. For many people, the pile-on of concerning news alerts had a sinister feel.
“We’re under attack in a way we’ve never seen before,” wrote Nalin Haley, a conservative influencer and son of Republican politician Nikki Haley, on Nov. 17. “This is an AI cyberattack.”
On Bluesky, Christopher Webb, a self-described “lifelong Dem” and party strategist, questioned whether the issues were connected.
“Coincidence??? 4 major banks reporting outages, a massive Microsoft disruption, and a nationwide FAA ground stop, all within days of each other,” he wrote Nov. 16.
The best available information points to mundane explanations such as routine maintenance, one-off problems or isolated cyberattacks, rather than an imminent systemic collapse or a coordinated attack on digital systems.
But why can that be hard to believe?
Human brains naturally detect patterns and reject uncertainty
The rapid-fire succession of events didn’t help. Neither did the timing of a planned, routine Nov. 17 test of the country’s Emergency Alert System.
Human brains are wired to make connections and spot statistical regularities in the world.
“Detecting patterns is important for perceiving the world and learning about cause and effect,” said Javier Granados Samayoa, a Texas Christian University psychology professor. This tendency “can sometimes lead people to see connections where none may exist.”
One paper about conspiracy thinking started with a coin toss. People who reported a tendency to notice patterns in a random string of coin tosses were more likely to also endorse conspiracy theories and supernatural beliefs.
Research also shows that when people lack control, they’re more likely to detect nonexistent patterns.
For people unable to access their work platforms or stuck at airports, powerlessness and confusion were all too familiar feelings. Those feelings contribute to embracing conspiracy theories.
“People are looking for ways to understand what is going on and they don’t like the uncertainty that often surrounds unfolding events,” said Karen Douglas, a University of Kent social psychology professor. “Also, a simple explanation is often not very appealing. People assume that there must somehow be a bigger explanation, or more going on than people know about.”
Human biases and social media platforms can intensify the anxieties
The flurry of frustration-inducing technical issues coupled with the known negativity bias observed across social media platforms can set people up to have outsized emotional reactions when things go wrong.
Negativity bias means that negative information has a stronger impact and people tend to think about it more, said Granados Samayoa. On social media, content is more likely to prompt engagement and go viral if it uses negative language or prompts a strong negative reaction.
Social media algorithms have continuously circulated some of the most alarming posts and conspiracy theories — an estimated 30% of which were pushed by suspected bots, including some with potential foreign influence, Axios reported.
Sharing conspiracy theories on social media is easy, fast and difficult to untangle.
“Once people believe in a conspiracy theory, it is often difficult to convince them otherwise,” Douglas said.
The events and concerns compounded as regular people and news reporters all began paying more attention to outages that would otherwise be routine. That’s commonly called frequency bias.
“United’s outage this afternoon is so pedestrian, it’d be a non-story if not for what’s happened the last four days,” Kyle Potter, an editor at Thrifty Traveler, wrote Nov. 16.
This story was provided by WABE media partner PolitiFact.

articles.title: What does Project 2025 say about the FAA and banking?
articles.text:
What does Project 2025 say about the FAA and banking?
What does Project 2025 say about the FAA and banking?
Banks
National News
Politics
Technology
What does Project 2025 say about the FAA and banking?
National News
Maria Briceño
PolitiFact
November 20th, 2026
A passenger moves through Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International airport as all flights are canceled or delayed, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, in Atlanta. (AP Photo/Mike Stewart)
After widespread technology disruptions to banking and air travel, some people are pointing to Project 2025.
“Just a reminder that what’s happening with the (Federal Aviation Administration) is planned and deliberate,” a TikTok narrator said.
A Facebook page from a group called The Democratic Coalition shared a photo of people lining up at what looks like an airport with text that said, “Remember, destroying the FAA is part of Project 2025.” Other posts on Facebook and Instagram make similar claims.
When major U.S. banks experienced widespread outages Nov. 16, social media users again invoked Project 2025.
“The bank outages make sense after the FAA grounding if you are aware of project 2025,” said David Ross Lawn, a digital creator with more than 600,000 followers, in a Nov. 16 Facebook post. “Banks were next in line on the agenda. They’re doing a speed run of Project 2025 because of the Blue Tsunami,” a reference to Democratic wins in the 2026 midterm elections.
Project 2025 was a presidential transition project led by the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank. The 900-page manual recommends detailed policies following a 2024 Republican presidential victory.
While some Project 2025 goals line up with descriptions in the social media posts, the posts also overstate what the project proposed. These goals do not have much to do with explanations offered for outages and the ground stop.
The nationwide ground stop, and what Project 2025 says about the FAA
The FAA’s Nov. 13 ground stop, which lasted about five hours, stemmed from the deployment of a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas, that caused “excessive data flooding the systems,” the FAA said.
Project 2025 would not “destroy” the FAA, as social posts claimed, but it would fundamentally reshape it. It recommends that the agency operate more like a business, reshape its funding sources and run separately from the Transportation Department.
The Trump administration hasn’t proposed restructuring the agency as the project outlines.
After the recent tech disruptions, multiple social media videos also pointed to pages 632 to 635 as evidence that Project 2025 aims to privatize certain parts of the FAA.
Aviation expert Edward Booth told PolitiFact that air traffic control services are already significantly privatized, with more than 50% of U.S. control towers run by private contractors. Booth drew a distinction between privatization and user fees for air traffic control services, which Project 2025 proposes.
“For nearly 100 years, all pilots in the U.S. have received (air traffic control) services free of charge,” Booth said. “Fuel and airline ticket taxes fund the system. Project 2025 urges charging fees for use of the system.”
Project 2025 says that at a minimum, the Air Traffic Organization should be separated from the FAA. The ATO is in charge of providing airspace navigation services to all of the U.S. and large portions of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans and the Gulf of Mexico.
“Organizations such as the FAA whose sole responsibility is public safety should be fully auditable and led by experts in their field or industry with oversight from DOT leadership,” page 633 of Project 2025 says.
It also calls for “completely restructuring the FAA’s funding system.” Instead of using taxes from aviation users, as it currently does, Project 2025 proposes that the FAA charge fees for air traffic services and issue long-term revenue bonds for major projects. Currently, the majority of the FAA’s funding comes from a trust fund that draws from taxes on domestic flight tickets, air cargo, plane fuel and other things.
Booth said Congress has consistently rejected direct user fees for air traffic control services. He predicted that if such fees are imposed, many general aviation pilots would not pay the fees and would fly without the air traffic control services.
After the ground stop, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, such as upgrading the telecommunication systems; the Trump administration said Nov. 17 it is seeking $50 billion more, on top of $12.5 billion that Congress approved in 2025.
Project 2025 aim to restructure the U.S. banking system?
JPMorgan Chase said it had longer than usual service times on Nov. 16 because of technical issues. A Chase spokesperson told CBS News that its services experienced a technical bug, not a cyber issue.
Bank of America customers also reported technical issues that day, but the bank told CBS the system was operating normally.
After the tech outages impacted banks and the FAA, a social media user connected the disruptions with Project 2025’s proposals. He said Project 2025 wants to “reshape federal banking oversight, consolidate regulatory functions and roll back major financial regulations.”
Project 2025 calls for restructuring the financial regulatory system. Chapter 22 supports legislation to merge the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the National Credit Union Administration and the Federal Reserve’s non-monetary supervisory and regulatory functions. It also calls for policymakers to create new charters for financial firms that reduce regulations, with these charters replacing government regulation.
In chapter 24, it recommends that neither interest rates nor the supply of money be controlled by the government. The Federal Reserve would be effectively abolished, and the Department of the Treasury would largely limit itself to handling the government’s money.
